title: Carmelo Anthony Defends Angel Reese’s Passion, Calls Critics “F‑‑ked Up” – Bleacher Report Reaction
body:
Ten‑time NBA All‑Star Carmelo Anthony stepped onto the national stage this week to champion Atlanta Dream guard Angel Reese, calling the backlash against her “f‑‑ked up” and insisting the young star’s fiery demeanor is a sign of passion, not a flaw. Speaking on his “7 PM in Brooklyn” podcast, the former NBA champion urged fans, commentators and even fellow athletes to look beyond the double‑standard that often shadows women’s basketball players, especially those who display confidence on the court. His remarks come as Reese prepares to lead the Dream into the 2026 WNBA Finals, a series that promises to be a defining moment for both the franchise and the league’s ongoing cultural conversation.

Reese, 22, has become one of the most polarizing figures in the WNBA since her breakout sophomore season with the Dream. Her aggressive play, outspoken interviews and unapologetic celebrations have drawn both fervent support and sharp criticism. While many fans praise her as a beacon of authenticity and a role model for younger athletes, detractors have labeled her “unprofessional” and “attention‑seeking,” often echoing language historically reserved for male athletes who exhibit similar intensity. Anthony’s defense highlighted this disparity, noting that comparable behavior from NBA stars is routinely celebrated as “passion” or “leadership.” He argued that the gendered lens applied to Reese not only undermines her contributions but also perpetuates a broader pattern of policing women’s expression in sport.

The former NBA MVP’s intervention is significant not only because of his stature but also because it underscores a growing alliance between former men’s‑league players and the women’s game. Over the past three years, several high‑profile NBA figures—including LeBron James, Kevin Durant and Stephen Curry—have publicly supported the WNBA, citing its competitive quality and cultural relevance. Anthony’s commentary adds to this momentum, suggesting that the league’s rising viewership and sponsorship deals are being bolstered by such cross‑sport advocacy. Moreover, his remarks arrive at a critical juncture: the Dream’s upcoming finals series against the Chicago Sky could be a watershed moment for the league’s marketability, especially as broadcasters negotiate new streaming contracts and advertisers seek authentic stories that resonate with younger demographics.

Critics of Anthony’s stance argue that his platform may inadvertently shift focus away from Reese’s on‑court performance, turning a personal narrative into a broader gender‑politics debate. Some analysts caution that while allyship is valuable, it should not eclipse the athletes’ own voices. Reese herself has consistently used her platform to discuss mental health, body positivity and the importance of staying true to one’s identity. In a recent interview, she emphasized that the “passion” fans see is rooted in years of hard work and a desire to elevate her team, not a calculated publicity stunt. Balancing these perspectives, many experts suggest that the conversation should celebrate both Reese’s skill set and her right to express herself without fear of undue scrutiny.

The episode also sheds light on the evolving role of media in shaping public perception of women’s sports. Social‑media platforms have amplified both praise and vitriol, often blurring the line between constructive criticism and personal attacks. Anthony’s public denouncement of the “f‑‑ked up” treatment of Reese may encourage other high‑profile athletes to speak out against misogynistic commentary, potentially fostering a more respectful discourse. At the same time, it raises questions about the responsibility of broadcasters and commentators to provide balanced coverage that acknowledges athletes’ humanity alongside their performance metrics.

As the Dream gear up for the finals, the spotlight on Reese will intensify, and so will the dialogue surrounding gender equity in sports. Anthony’s outspoken defense may serve as a catalyst for broader institutional changes—such as stricter policies against gender‑biased harassment and increased investment in women’s sports marketing. Whether the Dream clinches the championship or falls short, the narrative surrounding Angel Reese’s passion is likely to endure, prompting fans, pundits and league officials to reconsider how they evaluate and celebrate competitive fire across gender lines. The coming weeks will not only test the Dream’s on‑court resilience but also the sport’s capacity to evolve toward a more inclusive and equitable future.
